newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European analysts call EU, Boeing deal a draw.
newsitem.headline: European analysts call EU, Boeing deal a draw.

text.p: Both the European Commission and aircraft giant Boeing Co can claim victory in a battle of wills over the U.S. firm's $16 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp.
But many observers reckon the final deal, to be formally approved by the Commission next week, was not worth the risk of an all-out trade war in the first place.
"I'd say both sides got substantially what they wanted," Randolph Tritell, a partner with U.S. law firm Weil Gotschal & Manges, said.
"Boeing was able to have the essence of the deal approved and the Commission was able to obtain relief in areas it thought posed risks of anti-competitive results," he said.
"I don't think it has fundamentally changed the merger. It's a pretty empty victory really," said another lawyer, who was involved in the talks with the Commission.

The Commission recommended approving the merger on Wednesday after Boeing agreed to last-minute concessions aimed at ensuring Boeing would not abuse its strong market position and would leave airlines the choice of buying rival planes.
Analysts and antitrust lawyers agreed that the deal left the planned merger unscathed and did little to prevent Boeing from strengthening its position in the world's commercial aircraft sector.

But this was probably the best deal the Commission could expect, they said, since banning the merger would have provoked an explosive trade war between the United States and Europe which would have hit Boeing, its European rival Airbus Industrie, suppliers and customers.

The merger, with Boeing taking control of ailing McDonnell Douglas, increases Boeing's overall market share to 70 percent from 64 percent, leaving only Airbus to compete with it in the market for planes above 100-seats.
The Commission, using EU merger law, has traditionally forced companies to scale back merger plans whenever it found that dominant positions in the 15-nation bloc would be created or strengthened.
In the Boeing case, however, this was apparently not an option.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Wednesday that the Commission considered forcing Boeing to sell McDonnell's civil aviation operations, but there were no potential buyers.
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which earlier cleared the deal, also concluded the operations were not viable.
Van Miert also said European airlines, which operate MD planes, opposed cutting MD servicing and spare parts from the new merged group.
But his claim that the scrapping of Boeing's sole supply pacts with three U.S. airlines and pledge not to conclude any new ones for 10 years was a "spectacular" move, was over-gilding the lily.
The three carriers -- AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines -- have all said the decision would not alter their plans to buy Boeing planes.

Industry observers said the negotiations risked getting out of hand largely because Van Miert personalised the issue and upped the ante, by saying early on that Boeing's exclusivity pacts were "unacceptable" and that the company failed to take the Commission seriously.
"I don't see how Van Miert could have swallowed his words," an airline specialist said.
Van Miert, possibly with an eye on the European political ladder, has steadily flexed his muscles over huge corporate deals in telecoms and aerospace.
He has adopted a tough stance on the alliance between British Airways and American Airlines which is still awaiting EU clearance.
As these markets globalise, there is an increasing risk of dangerous frictions between the antitrust authorities on the two sides of the Atlantic.

In a bid to pre-empt further squabbles from escalating, European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan on Thursday joined with Van Miert to revive a 1996 EU proposal for an international competition authority within the World Trade Organisation.

"I have long believed that we need an international agreement on competition rules...Otherwise there are bound to be more and more clashes when powerful competition authorities seek to deal with the same case," he said.
